Gamma is not directional

Most 0DTE scalpers spend 2 years staring at 1-minute candles before realizing this.

At a live VIX of 21.40, options are pricing $SPX for 101.7 points of movement today. History says 56 of those points tend to print before 11:30 AM.

They see "VIX up a quarter point, market a little nervous."

A tiny group of vol desks sees a price that converts, with one division, into a points range for the session.

The VIX is the annualized implied volatility of 30-day SPX options, meaning the yearly move those options are priced for. Divide it by 15.87, the square root of 252 trading days, and you get the daily move: 21.40 / 15.87 = 1.35% a day. The average retail trader reads 21.40 as a fear gauge. A desk reads it as 101.7 points the market has already paid for.

Same number. Same screen. Completely opposite use.

The difference isn't the chart. It isn't the indicator. It's one division that turns a price into points.

Here's the map, from the 4:00 PM close to the open →

THE OVERNIGHT LEDGER:

→ 4:00 PM: SPX closes at 7,541.40 with VIX at 21.15. Every level below is anchored to that print.

→ Overnight: futures and SPY drift -20.4 SPX points, -0.27%. 20.4 / 101.7 = 0.20x of today's expected move, the one-session range options price in. That's not a gap. That's a fifth of the budget spent before the bell.

→ 08:16 ET: live VIX 21.40, a 100th percentile expected move for the last 60 sessions. Regime is FAST: VIX above 18.5 and dealer gamma negative.

→ 10:16 AM: Congressional Elections on the calendar, landing inside the morning window.

WHERE THE SHELVES MEET THE DEALER BOOK:

→ The dealer book is estimated from SPY open interest, the count of contracts still open. Net GEX, or gamma exposure, is -1.53B. Gamma is how fast an option's delta (its share-equivalent exposure) changes per point. When it is negative, dealers sell weakness and buy strength to stay hedged. That's not momentum. That's forced hedging stretching moves through levels.

→ 7,687, the flip line: the level where dealer gamma turns positive. Spot SPX equivalent is 7,531.5, which sits 155.1 points below it. The whole priced range lives in negative gamma.

→ 7,592 upper half-EM shelf: the modeled call wall is at 8,022 (SPY 800), 429.5 points higher. That's not resistance. That's open air.

→ 7,491 lower shelf: the modeled put wall is at 7,420 (SPY 740), 70.5 points below and just under the 7,440 range floor. That's not a random support line. That's where the band and the big put strike nearly meet.

→ The at-the-money straddle, a call plus a put at spot, costs 46.5 SPX points, about 4,653 dollars. That is 0.46x the expected move. With price flat, it decays to 38.7 by 11:30 AM and 28.9 by 1:30 PM. Lunch alone burns 9.9 points, 25.5% of what was left.

Now the part retail never computes.

7,541.40 x 0.2140 = 1,613.86

1,613.86 / 15.87 = 101.7 points

101.7 x 0.5 = 50.8 points

101.7 x 2.236 = 227.4 points

101.7 x 0.555 = 56.4 points before 11:30 AM

→ Daily range: 7,439.7 to 7,643.1

→ Half-EM shelves: 7,490.6 and 7,592.2

→ Weekly corridor: 7,314.0 to 7,768.8

→ Morning window: 56 of 102 points due by 11:30 AM

Base rate: 88% of the last 60 sessions closed inside the band priced before the bell. The median move was 36.7 points, 0.44x the priced move. Yesterday priced ±92.8 and moved -38.7, inside the band.

A shelf break WITH the move landing before 11:30 AM, while VIX holds above 21.15, is a FAST, negative gamma day spending its budget. A shelf break without it is the trap that chases the 7,440 extension after lunch, just as the 88% base rate pulls price back.

The scalper on 1-minute candles sees a red open. The map says 20.4 of 101.7 points are already gone, the put wall sits at 7,420, and the first real test is the 7,491 shelf.

The candle shows you where price was.

The VIX shows you how far it is paid to go.

Map these exact levels before every session, from the closing print to the live VIX.

The same SPX level can imply a very different hedge at 10 AM and 3 PM.

To understand why, start with the position.

The levels in this replay were shared last night in VS Pro. The framework behind them starts with understanding the market maker position and how its hedge requirements change through the session.

Whether market makers are long or short an option changes the direction of their hedge response. Understanding that response starts with understanding what they hold.

Once you understand the position, you can ask what happens to its delta as the session develops. Delta is the position's exposure to a move in the index. Market makers adjust their hedge as that exposure changes.

For example, consider a market maker who is long a call and short futures against it. As the index rises and the call gains delta, maintaining the hedge requires selling more futures. If the index falls and the call loses delta, maintaining the hedge requires buying futures back.

Reverse the option position and you reverse that hedge response.

That is why a gamma number only becomes useful once you understand the position behind it. And gamma alone cannot explain how the hedge changes while price stays in the same area and the clock advances.

Price moves. Time passes. Implied volatility changes.

Gamma, charm and vanna describe how each changes delta. Together, they help us work out the direction and rough size of the required hedge adjustment.

Even if SPX returns to the same level later in the day, less time remains and volatility may have changed. The position can have a different delta, so maintaining the hedge can require a different adjustment.

That's how I prepare for the session: understand the positions, then work through how the required hedging would evolve as price, time and volatility change. That gives me a way to understand the hedge path through the day. New trades can change the positions too.

Tests and balance levels are reference points for that process. Other expiries and other buying and selling still matter. A replay cannot establish who caused each move, and a level doesn't guarantee a reversal or a closing price.

Positions first. Then changing exposure. Then the hedge adjustment.

That's the sequence I teach in Dealer Hedging Dynamics. If you want to understand the reasoning behind these levels, the course starts with one option and its hedge, then builds toward reading a position through the session.

Educational analysis - not investment advice, and not a statement about any specific market participant's intent.

Knowing how to turn the VIX into $SPX points is the closest thing to an unfair advantage in 0DTE.

At 16.46, the VIX looks like a small, calm number.

Divide it by 15.87 and SPX is priced to move about 1.04% today, or 80.3 points.

Same VIX. Same chart. Two very different mornings.

The edge isn't a secret indicator. It isn't a faster phone. It's one division before the open.

Here's the full breakdown 👇

From fear gauge to points:

→ The VIX is the yearly move SPX options are pricing, in percent.

→ Dividing by 15.87 shrinks that yearly number down to one day.

→ Multiply by the SPX close and you get points.

7,744.06 x 16.46% / 15.87 = 80.3 points

Where that puts today's edges:

→ The priced range runs from 7,664 to 7,824.

→ The halfway lines sit at 7,704 and 7,784.

→ A target past 7,824 asks for more than the market priced.

→ The whole week is priced at plus or minus 179.6 points, so don't plan one morning as if it were the week.

Why today's walls can pull price:

→ Today is monthly OPEX, the day a big batch of monthly options expires.

→ The model floor is 7,700, a big put strike.

→ The model ceiling is 7,785, a big call strike, almost on the 7,784 halfway line.

→ Open interest means contracts still open, and a large amount of it rolls off at the close.

Once those walls are gone, tomorrow's VIX will draw a brand new box.

My least favourite condor fix

Rolling up the untested side of an iron condor is probably one of my least favourite ways to adjust it.

Say the market's rallied towards your call spread. One fix is to buy back the put spread and sell a new one higher up, closer to spot, to collect a bit more premium.

The problem for me is the move usually builds through the life of the trade. So by the time you roll up, the extra premium you get just doesn't feel attractive enough. And you've moved your short puts closer, so if the market sells off back through them you could be in trouble.

That doesn't mean it's a bad idea. It can work. My instinct is just to not generally want to do it that way.

And to be honest, I'm preaching discipline here, but there've been times I've let one of these snowball because I was stubborn, or I wasn't watching it closely enough and the market gapped. 

You will make mistakes. You just have to make sure you learn from them.

Most 0DTE traders will never learn this about the dealer flip line.

At the open, $SPY at 752.68 puts SPX near 7,547, which is 88.4 points below the switch at 7,636. Every dip you buy down here is being sold into by the people holding the other side of your options.

They see "a normal pullback, a level to buy."

A tiny group of vol desks sees which side of the switch price is on, and that decides whether dealers calm the move or feed it.

Dealers are the firms that sell options and then hedge with stock or futures. Gamma is how fast an option's delta changes, and delta is how much the option moves per point of SPX. When dealers are net short gamma, every move forces them to trade in the same direction as price. Today net SPY GEX, the map of dealer hedging across strikes, is estimated at -1.70B from SPY open interest, the count of contracts still open. That means negative gamma. The average retail trader reads a red open as a discount. A desk reads it as a forced seller getting louder.

Same tape. Same red candle. Completely opposite conclusion.

The difference isn't the chart pattern. It isn't the indicator. It's which side of the gamma switch price is sitting on.

Here's the map, strike by strike →

WHERE THE SWITCH SITS:

→ SPY 761.50, or SPX 7,636. This is the flip line, the price where dealer gamma changes sign. Above it, dealers buy dips and sell rips, which dampens moves. Below it, they sell drops and buy rips, which stretches them. That's not a support level. That's a regime switch.

→ SPX 7,547, spot. It sits 88.4 points under the switch. That's not "a little weak." That's fully inside fuel mode.

→ SPX 7,641, the top of today's full priced range. The flip at 7,636 sits just 5 points under that edge. Price would need nearly a full expected move up just to reach the calm side.

WHAT DEALERS MUST DO BELOW IT:

→ On a drop from 7,547, short-gamma dealers sell futures to stay hedged as their delta shifts. Each tick lower brings more selling. That's not panic. That's arithmetic.

→ On a rip toward 7,591, they must buy into it. That's not a breakout. That's hedging chasing price.

→ The regime is tagged FAST: VIX at 21.03 is above 18.5 and net gamma is negative. That's not noise. That's the switch and the volatility pointing the same way.

THE SHELVES AND WALLS AROUND IT:

→ SPX 7,491, the lower half-EM shelf. The expected move is the range options price for one session. A break here has no dealer cushion behind it. That's not a dip. That's an air pocket.

→ SPX 7,420, the put wall at SPY 740. It sits 71.4 points below the 7,491 shelf. Near the big put strike, dealer buying tends to cushion dips. That's the first real brake.

→ SPX 8,022, the call wall at SPY 800. It sits 430.3 points above the 7,591 shelf. That's not a ceiling for today. That's irrelevant until the switch flips.

Now the part retail never computes.

(752.68 - 761.50) x 10.03 = 88.4 SPX points below the flip line

7,541.40 x 0.2103 = 1,585.96

1,585.96 / 15.87 = 99.9 points of expected move (15.87 is the square root of 252 trading days)

99.9 x 0.5 = 50.0 points

→ Half-EM shelves: 7,491.4 and 7,591.4

→ Full range: 7,441.5 to 7,641.3

→ Flip line: 7,636, inside the range but only at its upper edge

→ Put wall: 7,420, below the full range floor

A drop through 7,491 WITH price still under 7,636 is a move dealers are forced to feed toward 7,420. A drop through 7,491 without that negative gamma behind it is the trap that gets you short into a dealer bid.

The trader buying the opening dip near 7,547 thinks they're early. They're 88.4 points on the wrong side of the switch, with no wall until 7,420.

The chart shows you where price bounced last time.

The switch tells you who is forced to trade next.
